title: the Rajasuya
hook: Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna walk into Jarasandha's city dressed as snatakas, refuse his welcome, and name themselves at midnight
carry: they gave their names, and their reason

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Rajasuya nearly given up, then Jarasandha's birth in two halves. Your line was the one joined by Jara.

Three men walk into the capital of Magadha dressed as snatakas, young brahmanas who've just finished their studies. They wear garlands and sandal paste. They don't come in by the main gate, a strange way for students to arrive anywhere. And they walk straight into the king's presence. Jarasandha stands to receive them as honored guests. He has no idea that Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna are standing in his hall.
screen: `DRESSED AS SNATAKAS.` → `NOT BY THE MAIN GATE.` → `THE KING STANDS TO GREET THEM.`

segments.voice: Jarasandha does everything a good host should: water, honors, a seat. They won't take it. Krishna speaks for the group: my two companions are keeping a vow of silence until midnight. Then they'll speak. So the king leaves, comes back at midnight, and asks what he's been holding. Snatakas don't wear garlands and paste like this. Your arms are marked like the arms of men who draw bows. You came in by a wrong way. And you refused my worship. Who are you? Krishna's answer is careful, and honest. A snataka enters a friend's house by its gate, and an enemy's by another way. And we don't accept worship from an enemy. Jarasandha is puzzled: I've never wronged you. Then Krishna names the wrong. You've captured kings and mean to offer them up as a sacrifice. We've come to free them. And he tells the king exactly who they are. The disguise gets them through the door, but once inside they don't hide why they came. They refuse the welcome; some readers say accepting it would have made them guests, and a guest can't rightly fight his host. They wait until he asks, then give their names and their reason. Jarasandha answers just as plainly. I took those kings in war, and I won't let them go out of fear. Fight me, one of you, or two, or all three. He looks the three of them over, and chooses Bhima.
screen: `THEY REFUSE THE WELCOME.` · `MIDNIGHT: WHO ARE YOU?` · `A FOE'S HOUSE, ANOTHER WAY IN.` · `NAMES AND REASONS, PLAINLY.` · then, large: `HE CHOOSES BHIMA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a hard conversation you've had, or one that's coming, and notice what you're carrying into it: anything disguised, any welcome you'd accept that you don't mean to keep. Picture saying your reason plainly, the way Krishna does at midnight. It only needs to be clear to you for now.
The Rajasuya. Today it runs through Jarasandha's hall at midnight, where three guests refuse his welcome and tell him why they've come.
Your line: they gave their names, and their reason. The disguise opened the door; the truth came after. That's day seven hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: A snataka is a student who has completed Vedic study and taken the ritual bath that ends it; Hindu tradition sets out a snataka's conduct, which is why Jarasandha notices that his guests don't look the part.

chat.says: Why did Krishna and the others refuse Jarasandha's welcome?
options: They came as his enemies, and wouldn't take worship from a man they'd fight.
They thought the food was poisoned, as the lac house had been a trap.
Snatakas are forbidden to sit in any king's hall, so they stood.
chat.meaning: Krishna said a snataka enters a foe's house by another way and won't accept worship from a foe. They had come to free the captive kings.

snatakas.meaning: students who've finished Vedic study and its closing bath

Jarasandha.meaning: king of Magadha, who holds kings captive

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Jarasandha-vadha Parva (the journey to Girivraja in snataka dress; the vow of silence until midnight; Krishna's answer; Jarasandha chooses Bhima)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm: snataka dress, garlands and sandal paste; entry not by the main gate; Jarasandha receiving them with honors.
Confirm Krishna's statement that his companions keep silence until midnight, and Jarasandha's midnight questions, including the bowstring marks on their arms.
Confirm Krishna's reply that a snataka enters a friend's house by the gate and a foe's by another way, and won't accept worship from a foe.
Confirm Jarasandha's reply: took the kings in war, won't release them from fear, offers to fight one, two or all three, and chooses Bhima.
The trapdoor's third floor (refusing worship keeps them from being guests) is an interpretation; a Keeper may wish to soften it.

Audit: the teach said "nobody lies about anything" once inside, which overstates (the disguise and the midnight delay are themselves concealment); now "they don't hide why they came". Trapdoor third floor now attributes the guest reading to some readers and keeps the text's own reason.
Details such as breaking drums on Chaityaka hill were left out as uncertain.
Editor pass: cut the unsourced 'they carry no visible weapons'; the teach's claim that guests can't fight their host is now framed as some readers' view, not the narrator's.
